title: Serpents and doves (Matthew 10:16–33)
hookLine: wise as serpents, harmless as doves; not a sparrow falls without your Father
tomorrow: how does a speech about a sword end with a cup of water?

cards: Some advice comes in two halves that seem to fight: be kind, but don't be a doormat. Jesus gives it to the twelve with animals, right after the packing list.
"Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves."
They'll be brought before governors and kings, he warns, and when it happens, they're to "take no thought how or what ye shall speak." Not much of a recruiting pitch.

teach.b: Two animals with opposite reputations in the Bible. Back in Genesis, "the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field."
The dove is the bird Noah sent from the ark, and at Jesus' baptism the Spirit came down like one. He doesn't ask the twelve to pick.
He asks for both at once. Wise alone can slide into cunning. Harmless alone can walk straight into the wolves.
Together: a person who sees the trap clearly and still won't set one.

Then he turns from danger to small birds: "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows."
One to tell a friend tonight: two sparrows for one small coin, and still not one falls unnoticed.
That's what lets sheep stay gentle among wolves. Not that the danger is small, but that they aren't alone in it.

how: Some Christians turn to wise as serpents, harmless as doves when facing hard dealings at work or in public life, and some pray Matthew 10:29–31 in times of fear.

o: a warning to keep away from snakes and birds
being clear-eyed and gentle at the same time
choosing cleverness over kindness when it counts

games.q: the animals of the sending — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus told the twelve to choose: wise or harmless
both at once: wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Jesus promised the twelve their road would be safe
sheep in the midst of wolves, brought before governors and kings.
Jesus says not one sparrow falls without your Father
and the very hairs of your head are all numbered.

games.q: a coworker keeps presenting your work as his in meetings. what fits wise as serpents, harmless as doves?
o: keep clear records and speak up calmly, without a jab.
take credit for his work next time, to even it out.
stay quiet forever, because doves never make a fuss.
games.why: Jesus asks for both at once: see the trap clearly, and still don't set one.

practice: Listen for the smallest sound you can find: a bird outside, a tick in the wall, the hum of the fridge. Rest your attention there as if it mattered, the way Matthew says not one sparrow falls unnoticed.

wordCard.voice: Serpents and doves. Wise enough to see the trap, harmless enough never to set one.

orig.note: Greek: wise, sensible, shrewd. the word in Matthew 10:16 for wise as serpents.

carryVoice: Keep this one: wise and harmless, both at once, among sparrows that are counted. Another week, done.
